To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

egg laying by elm leaf beetls induces the transcription of defense genes in elms, and that the induced genes can be used as markers for the identification of egg-induced defense genes in other plant–insect systems.
elm responds to egg laying by the herbivore elm leaf beetle with the emission of volatile signals and the activation of jasmonic-acid dependent defense responses.

the transcriptional profile in the European elm (Ulmaceae) is altered after egg laying by the Elm Leaf Beetle (Coleoptera: Chrysomelidae), and that many defense genes are up-regulated, including pathogen related proteins, and genes involved in the jasmonic acid pathway.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of genes involved in plant defense against herbivore eggs and the elucidation of the mechanisms of egg-induced defense gene regulation in a natural plant–insect association.
the identification of genes and pathways involved in egg-induced defenses in plants and will help to elucidate the molecular mechanisms of egg-induced indirect plant defense.
identifying genes that are involved in plant defense mechanisms against herbivore eggs.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
egg laying by the insect induces the expression of many defense genes in the host tree, which is in accordance with the hypothesis of egg-induced defense in plants.

the egg-induced defense of the elm is a complex process involving a wide range of biological processes and that the defense response is directed not only against eggs, but also against other herbivorous insects.
the transcriptional response of elms to egg laying is highly complex, and that the defense response is only a small part of the total transcriptional changes induced.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the elm leaf beetle eggs trigger a complex response in elm, which involves the activation of defense genes and a reduction of primary metabolic pathways, and which is likely to be coordinated by the plant hormone jasmonic acid.

egg-induced defenses in elm are likely to be a complex network of transcriptional events that involve many genes and biological processes, which may be orchestrated by phytohormones and/or other signaling molecules.
the elm leaf beetle eggs induce a strong defense reaction in the host plant.
The main takeaway from our work is that
egg laying by herbivorous insects is a potent trigger for plant defense, which may be used by plants to defend themselves against other herbivore species.
the egg-induced transcriptional changes in elm are very different from the ones induced by herbivore feeding, suggesting the activation of different defense mechanisms.
